name: Eccentric Heel Drops
rationale: Slow eccentric loading through the Achilles is the most evidence-backed intervention for both preventing and rehabilitating Achilles tendinopathy. Performing them on a step edge maximises the lengthening range available.
evidence: Strong RCT evidence (Alfredson protocol) for Achilles tendinopathy management; also effective as prehab in runners with high weekly mileage.

name: Single-Leg Calf Raises
muscleText: Gastrocnemius (straight-knee variant), soleus (bent-knee variant), Achilles tendon
rationale: Heavy single-leg calf raises build the plantarflexion strength needed to propel body weight through the toe-off phase of each stride. Progressing from double-leg to single-leg matches the unilateral demand of running.
evidence: Recommended in consensus guidelines for Achilles and plantar fascia load management in distance runners.

name: Soleus Stretch (Bent-Knee Calf Stretch)
rationale: The soleus inserts directly into the Achilles and is often tighter than the gastrocnemius in runners due to the bent-knee position of the lower leg at ground contact. The bent-knee variant isolates the soleus specifically.
evidence: Commonly prescribed alongside eccentric loading in Achilles tendinopathy management protocols.

name: Hip Abductor Strengthening (Side-Lying Leg Raise)
muscleText: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae (TFL)
rationale: Weakness in the hip abductors — especially glute medius — causes contralateral pelvic drop during the stance phase of running, increasing IT band tension and knee valgus stress. Targeted strengthening corrects this movement fault.
evidence: Widely recommended for IT band syndrome prevention and management; hip abductor weakness is a consistent finding in runners with ITBS.

name: Foam Roll IT Band / TFL
muscleText: Tensor fasciae latae (TFL), iliotibial band, lateral quadriceps
rationale: Foam rolling the lateral thigh and TFL reduces local tissue tension and improves tolerance to compression at the lateral knee. Focus rolling on the TFL at the hip rather than the band itself for greatest effect.
evidence: Modest evidence for short-term pain relief and mobility; most useful combined with hip strengthening rather than in isolation.

name: Clamshells
targetTissue: Gluteus medius, deep hip external rotators
muscleText: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, piriformis, obturator externus
rationale: Clamshells target the hip external rotators and glute medius in a controlled range of motion, building the rotational stability that prevents knee tracking problems. Resistance bands increase the training effect without adding joint load.
evidence: Commonly prescribed for patellofemoral pain and IT band syndrome; effective for activating glute med in runners.

name: Tibialis Anterior Raises (Heel Walks / Toe Raises)
muscleText: Tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus
rationale: Shin splints often result from an imbalance between calf strength and anterior compartment endurance. Strengthening the tibialis anterior reduces the decelerating eccentric load on the muscle during the foot-strike phase.
evidence: Recommended in shin-splint (medial tibial stress syndrome) prevention and return-to-run programmes.

name: Toe Taps
muscleText: Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, peroneus tertius
rationale: Rapid toe taps build dorsiflexion endurance and neuromuscular control, training the anterior compartment at a cadence more specific to running than slow isolated raises. Useful as a dynamic warm-up drill for athletes with shin-splint history.
evidence: Used in shin-splint rehabilitation as a low-load, high-repetition endurance stimulus for the anterior compartment.

name: Standing Calf Stretch (Straight-Leg)
rationale: A tight gastrocnemius increases stress on the anterior compartment by limiting dorsiflexion range, forcing compensatory tibial loading. Regular calf stretching restores dorsiflexion mobility and reduces the eccentric burden on the shin muscles.
evidence: Standard component of shin-splint management; reduced ankle dorsiflexion ROM is a known risk factor for MTSS.

name: Single-Leg Glute Bridge
muscleText: Gluteus maximus (primary), gluteus medius, hamstrings, core stabilisers
rationale: Single-leg glute bridges replicate the hip-extension demand of running in a controlled, low-impact position. They build glute max strength and expose pelvic stability weaknesses that contribute to hip drop and knee overload during running.
evidence: Effective for glute activation and hip strength development; frequently used in running injury prevention programmes.

name: Lateral Band Walk
muscleText: Gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae
rationale: Lateral band walks are one of the most targeted ways to fatigue the glute medius, the muscle responsible for keeping the pelvis level during single-leg stance. Consistent use closes the hip-strength gap that causes IT band and knee problems.
evidence: Strong activation evidence for glute medius; recommended in hip strengthening protocols for distance runners.

name: Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch
muscleText: Iliopsoas, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae
rationale: Extended periods of sitting shorten the hip flexors, which can create anterior pelvic tilt and reduce glute activation during running. Releasing hip flexor tension improves stride length and allows the glutes to fire more powerfully.
evidence: Commonly prescribed in runner prehab; hip flexor tightness is associated with reduced glute activation and increased lumbar stress.

name: Dead Bug
targetTissue: Transverse abdominis, multifidus, deep core stabilisers
muscleText: Transverse abdominis, multifidus, rectus abdominis, diaphragm
rationale: Dead bugs train the deep core to maintain a neutral spine while the limbs move — exactly the challenge the core faces during running. The anti-extension demand builds spinal stability without loading the lumbar spine in compression.
evidence: Widely recommended by physiotherapists for low-back pain prevention; effective for deep core activation without lumbar loading.

name: Bird Dog
targetTissue: Multifidus, erector spinae, glutes, core stabilisers
muscleText: Multifidus, erector spinae, gluteus maximus, transverse abdominis
rationale: Bird dogs challenge the lumbar stabilisers under diagonal loading, replicating the rotational demand placed on the trunk during running. They build the co-activation between glutes and low-back muscles needed for a stiff, efficient running torso.
evidence: Core component of the McGill Big 3 for low-back health; strong evidence for lumbar stabilisation in rehabilitation and prevention.

name: Cat-Cow
targetTissue: Lumbar spine, thoracic spine, erector spinae
muscleText: Erector spinae, multifidus, abdominals, thoracic paraspinals
rationale: Cat-cow gently mobilises the entire spinal column through flexion and extension, reducing stiffness that builds up with high training volume or prolonged sitting. It is an ideal warm-up or cool-down movement for runners with low-back tension.
evidence: Universally recommended for spinal mobility; effective as a low-load warm-up to reduce perceived low-back stiffness before activity.
